title: Infertility - History, Differentials and Diagnosis
patient_instructions: You are Emma Roberts, a 27-year-old primary school teacher, presenting to a GP because you and your partner have been trying to conceive for 12 months without success, and you are worried. Your periods are regular (28-30 day cycles). You were on the combined oral contraceptive pill for years and stopped it a year ago. You have one long-term partner. You do NOT time intercourse to any particular part of your cycle and are not sure when your fertile window is; you have sex roughly once a week. You have no excess hair growth, no acne, no abnormal bleeding, no pain with sex. You had your appendix removed at age 10 (uncomplicated). Your partner has never had a semen (sperm) analysis and has no children. Your BMI is 24. No thyroid, weight, vision or breast-discharge symptoms. If asked about your concern: 'I'm scared there's something wrong with me and I'll never have a baby.' Affect: anxious but cooperative. Only reveal the intercourse-timing and partner semen-analysis details when specifically asked.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. Emma Roberts, a 27-year-old woman, presents because she has been unable to conceive after 12 months of trying. In the next 8 minutes: take a focused history (remembering infertility is assessed as a couple), examination findings will be provided on the screen, then explain the likely contributing factors and the investigations you would arrange for both partners. No physical examination is required.
examiner_instructions: Look for a couple-based approach. Reward a structured history: duration of trying, intercourse frequency and timing/fertile-window awareness, partner factors (previous children, chronic illness, prior semen analysis), menstrual/ovulatory history, and screening across the differential groups (hypothalamic-pituitary, thyroid/prolactin, ovarian [PCOS/POI], tubal, uterine, cervical, male). Examination is normal (BMI 24). Strong candidates avoid over-attributing infertility to the childhood appendicectomy; they identify sub-optimal intercourse timing/frequency and the absent semen analysis as the immediately correctable factors, and state up to 40-50% of infertility involves a male factor so a semen analysis is a mandatory early investigation. They should list day 2-4 FSH/LH, TSH, prolactin, androgens, AMH, transvaginal ultrasound AND mid-luteal (day-21) progesterone to confirm ovulation, plus preconception care and a referral threshold. Use terms COCP and premature ovarian insufficiency (POI). Prompt if needed: 'What one test confirms she is ovulating?' (mid-luteal progesterone).

criteria: Explores duration of trying, intercourse frequency and fertile-window awareness/timing
Takes partner history early (previous children, chronic illness, prior semen analysis)
Menstrual/ovulatory history and 5 Ps adapted for infertility
Screens differential groups: hypothalamic (stress/exercise/eating), thyroid/prolactin, PCOS/POI, tubal/pelvic surgery, uterine/cervical
Frames infertility as a couple-based problem and notes up to 40-50% involve a male factor
Identifies sub-optimal intercourse timing/frequency and the absent partner semen analysis as the leading correctable factors
Presents childhood appendicectomy only as a possible minor contributor, not the leading diagnosis
Arranges concurrent semen analysis for the partner as a mandatory early investigation
Requests female work-up: day 2-4 FSH/LH, TSH, prolactin, androgens, AMH, transvaginal ultrasound AND mid-luteal (day-21) progesterone to confirm ovulation

Provides preconception care (folic acid, rubella/varicella serology, cervical screening, BMI, smoking/alcohol) and defines referral threshold (no conception after 12 months if <35, or 6 months if >=35, or earlier with risk factors)
Empathic, non-blaming and involves the couple; checks understanding
Explains the fertile window and lifestyle advice clearly

red_flags: Age >=35 or known risk factors (oligo/amenorrhoea, prior PID/pelvic surgery, abnormal semen analysis) warranting earlier specialist referral
Amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea or galactorrhoea suggesting endocrine cause (PCOS, premature ovarian insufficiency, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease)
Symptoms of premature ovarian insufficiency (hot flushes, family history) in a young woman
Failure to investigate the male partner - a common and correctable omission that delays diagnosis
australian_guidelines: RANZCOG/RACGP fertility assessment: investigate the couple concurrently; semen analysis is a mandatory early test as up to 40-50% of cases involve a male factor
Confirm ovulation with a mid-luteal (day-21 or 7 days before expected period) serum progesterone in addition to day 2-4 FSH/LH, TSH, prolactin, androgens, AMH and transvaginal ultrasound
Refer to a fertility specialist if no conception after 12 months (age <35), after 6 months (age >=35), or earlier with known risk factors
RACGP preconception care: folic acid, rubella and varicella serology, up-to-date cervical screening, BMI optimisation and smoking/alcohol cessation
learning_objectives: Assess infertility as a couple with a structured, grouped differential
Prioritise the immediately correctable factors (intercourse timing/frequency and semen analysis)
Select an evidence-based investigation panel including ovulation confirmation
Apply Australian referral thresholds and preconception care
key_points: The fertile window is roughly days 10-17 of a 28-day cycle; advise intercourse every 1-2 days across this period
Use current terminology: COCP and premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), not 'COPs' or 'POF'
Mid-luteal progesterone is the single most useful test to confirm ovulation and is easily forgotten
An uncomplicated childhood appendicectomy is a weak cause of tubal-factor infertility

citations.claim: Female subfertility is assessed by taking a general and reproductive history from each partner, framing the couple-based approach and diagnostic groups the case uses.

Thyroid dysfunction (e.g. thyrotoxicosis with weight loss, tremor, goitre) is a recognised endocrine contributor to menstrual/ovulatory disturbance, supporting thyroid screening and TSH investigation.
Systematic clinical assessment underpins the infertility work-up and physical examination.
